name: Cancel Amazon Prime
shortDescription: One account, six companies you're also funding.
longDescription: Prime membership funds Amazon's retail, logistics, cloud, advertising, and media arms in one subscription. Cancelling it is a five-minute account setting, not a boycott of every seller who happens to list there.

name: Swap the household aisle
shortDescription: Detergent, toothpaste, razors. Done once, done forever.
longDescription: A handful of purchases repeat every month without a second thought — laundry, dish, and personal care basics. Pick one replacement brand for each and the switch never has to be re-decided.

name: Learn who owns your brands
shortDescription: Twenty minutes on the ten things you buy most. Then you never look it up again.
longDescription: A dozen conglomerates own most of what's on a supermarket shelf. Angel Soft is Koch. Oreo and Philadelphia are Mondelez. Oral-B and Gillette are Procter & Gamble. Spend twenty minutes learning the ownership tree for the ten things you buy most — after that you stop needing to check, and you can explain it to other people.

name: Research a company before you spend
shortDescription: Ownership, ethics, and political donations — before checkout, not after.
longDescription: Ethical Consumer, Goods Unite Us, OpenSecrets, and product-origin scanners can tell you who you're paying and what they fund, before you've committed to the purchase.

name: Switch your regular grocery retailer
shortDescription: Move your default cart to a co-op or independent grocer.
longDescription: Most grocery spending goes on autopilot to whichever store is closest or already saved in an app. Picking a different default — a co-op, a regional chain, a local market — redirects a recurring, not one-time, amount.

name: Redirect one purchase to a local business
shortDescription: Pick one thing you'd normally buy from a large retailer and buy it local instead.
longDescription: Doesn't have to be everything, every time. One redirected purchase — a gift, a repair, a specialty item — is real money that went somewhere else.

name: Audit every recurring subscription
shortDescription: One sitting, one list, one clear picture of what's billing you.
longDescription: Bank and card statements make this a fifteen-minute exercise: list every recurring charge, then decide, cancel, or replace each one deliberately instead of by inertia.

name: Cancel Netflix
shortDescription: One streaming subscription, cancelled or paused.
longDescription: A settings-page cancellation. Note what, if anything, replaced it — that's the part worth sharing.

name: Cancel Disney+
shortDescription: One streaming subscription, cancelled or paused.
longDescription: A settings-page cancellation. Note what, if anything, replaced it — that's the part worth sharing.

name: Cancel another streaming service
shortDescription: Max, Paramount+, Apple TV+ — whichever one you're not watching.
longDescription: The third one is usually the easiest: the one you forgot you still had.

name: Move your cloud storage
shortDescription: Photos and files, migrated to an EU-based or nonprofit provider.
longDescription: The migration is the only real friction — most providers have a straightforward export/import path. Do it once and the monthly charge simply moves.

name: Switch your music subscription
shortDescription: Same playlists, different company.
longDescription: Most services let you export playlists before cancelling, so the switch doesn't cost you your library.

name: Open an account at a credit union
shortDescription: Member-owned, not shareholder-owned.
longDescription: Opening the account is the fast part — most of the work is deciding it's worth doing. Ten to thirty minutes, often online.

name: Move your primary checking account
shortDescription: Your everyday deposits are working capital your bank lends and invests.
longDescription: Direct deposit and autopay migration is the actual work here — most banks have a switch kit that automates it.

name: Switch to a credit-union-issued card
shortDescription: Same rails, different lender behind the card.
longDescription: Update your saved payment methods after the new card arrives — that's the whole switch.

name: Ask your bank one direct question
shortDescription: What do they lend to, and would they say so in writing?
longDescription: A single, specific, written question to your bank's customer service or branch — about their lending priorities — creates a record and costs one email.

name: Review and cut your bank fees
shortDescription: Monthly maintenance, overdraft, and ATM fees add up quietly.
longDescription: Most fee schedules are negotiable or avoidable once you know they exist — call and ask, or switch to an account type without them.

name: Check who finances ICE detention
shortDescription: Some banks have arranged billions for private detention operators.
longDescription: Look up whether your bank appears on financing lists for private prison and detention operators, and move your account if it does. If you do, tell them why.

name: Ask what your pension holds
shortDescription: You may own what you're boycotting.
longDescription: Retirement plans are handed to you with a default fund lineup nobody explains. Request the holdings list — it's a right, not a favor.

name: Request your plan's fund lineup in writing
shortDescription: A paper trail beats a phone call you can't cite later.
longDescription: Most providers have a standard disclosure document — ask for it by name so you have something concrete to review or share.

name: Move a discretionary investment account
shortDescription: Not the whole retirement plan — just the account you control directly.
longDescription: A brokerage or taxable account you manage yourself is the easiest one to move to a values-screened fund, since there's no employer plan administrator in the way.

name: Learn what your index funds actually hold
shortDescription: A total-market fund owns almost everything, including what you'd rather not.
longDescription: Fund fact sheets list top holdings publicly. Twenty minutes tells you what you're already exposed to, before you decide anything about it.

name: Ask your employer about the plan provider
shortDescription: HR can usually name the administrator and the fund menu.
longDescription: One email to HR or benefits, asking who administers the retirement plan and what the default fund is, on the record.

name: Redirect one booking
shortDescription: One trip, rerouted to a different destination or operator.
longDescription: Inbound tourism spending shows up in public monthly statistics — one redirected booking is a real, countable number, not a symbolic gesture.

name: Switch your rental car provider
shortDescription: Compare on the way to checkout — it's usually the same three clicks.
longDescription: Rental comparison sites make this close to a wash on price, so the switch mostly costs the habit of always picking the same one.

name: Choose rail or transit over a flagged airline
shortDescription: For one trip where it's realistically an option.
longDescription: Doesn't have to be every trip — one deliberate substitution, on a route where rail is genuinely viable, is the whole action.

name: Delay a discretionary vehicle purchase
shortDescription: Public, peaceful, and about spending — nothing else.
longDescription: Any acknowledgment of vehicle-brand demonstrations in this app follows the same non-violence framing as the source campaign: peaceful, no property damage, focused on spending decisions.

name: Log a trip you already redirected
shortDescription: Already changed a booking? Make it count here too.
longDescription: If you'd already made this call before finding this list, log it — the collective count only works if real, already-taken actions get counted.

name: Ask what your workplace buys
shortDescription: One organisation switching outweighs a thousand individual consumers.
longDescription: Your employer, council, union, club, or congregation all sign contracts. Asking who holds them, and from whom, is the first step — someone has to raise it.

name: Propose one procurement change
shortDescription: A specific vendor swap, put forward formally.
longDescription: A written proposal — to a workplace committee, an HOA board, a club, or a congregation — naming one specific contract to reconsider.

name: Ask your local government one procurement question
shortDescription: Council contracts are public record — asking makes that visible.
longDescription: A single specific question, submitted through a council's public comment or contact process, about a specific contract or vendor relationship.

name: Attend one institutional or shareholder meeting
shortDescription: Public comment periods and shareholder meetings are open for a reason.
longDescription: Council sessions, shareholder meetings, and public hearings usually have an open comment window — showing up, even without speaking, is the action.

name: Submit a public comment on a purchasing decision
shortDescription: Written, on the record, tied to a specific decision.
longDescription: Most public bodies have a formal comment process for procurement decisions — using it creates a record that a hallway conversation doesn't.

name: Register to vote, or confirm you're still registered
shortDescription: Institutional power runs through elected ones too.
longDescription: A registration check takes minutes and is the highest-leverage single action most people can take toward the institutions that set the rules everything else operates under.

name: Share brand-ownership research with a coworker
shortDescription: The information only spreads if someone hands it over.
longDescription: Send one person the ownership research you already did — a link, a screenshot, a two-line summary. That's the whole action.

name: Delete or deactivate one attention platform
shortDescription: Your attention, your posts, and your data are the product.
longDescription: Withdraw the supply. A single platform, deleted or deactivated, is the whole action — no need to leave everything at once.

name: Switch to a chronological feed
shortDescription: Where the setting exists, the algorithm is optional.
longDescription: Most major platforms still offer a non-algorithmic timeline option, buried a few taps deep. Turning it on changes what gets fed to you, immediately.

name: Move your news reading to a source you pay directly
shortDescription: Fund the alternative with what an ad-funded feed used to cost you.
longDescription: A direct subscription to a source you trust replaces an ad-funded feed's business model with one that doesn't depend on holding your attention as long as possible.

name: Set a hard daily limit on one platform
shortDescription: A device-level limit, not a promise to yourself.
longDescription: Phone-level app timers are enforced by the device, not willpower — set one on the platform you use most.

name: Unfollow one advertiser-funded feed
shortDescription: One account, one unfollow, one fewer ad impression counted against you.
longDescription: Small and specific on purpose — the smallest version of this action still counts.

name: Delete one attention app for a week
shortDescription: A real, checkable week off — not a vague intention to cut back.
longDescription: Delete the app, not just the habit — for one full week. Check back in when the week's up.
